summary.text: A 50-year-old morbidly obese man (BMI 40.1 kg/m²) with chronic essential hypertension, atrial flutter and type 2 diabetes mellitus was found unresponsive by his roommate after an unwitnessed seizure and taken by EMS to the emergency department in a postictal state. He had another seizure on arrival (witnessed generalized tonic-clonic with bladder incontinence per the abstract) and was admitted. He denied prior seizure disorder or osteoporosis.

Workup showed an elevated non-fasting blood glucose of 337 mg/dL, no acute cerebrovascular events on CT of the brain, no epileptiform activity on EEG and a non-focal neurological examination. Initial treatment was intravenous lorazepam 2 mg and intravenous levetiracetam 1,000 mg. He was discharged with levetiracetam 500 mg and aspirin 81 mg (CHA₂DS₂-VASc score 2) and no lumbar spine imaging.

Three days later he returned to the emergency department with severe bilateral lower back pain. Lumbar CT during the second admission showed acute to subacute compression injuries; MRI showed paraspinal soft-tissue edema and compression deformities at L1, L4 and L5 without spinal canal stenosis, and portable radiographs showed increased radiodensity at these levels. Citing absence of osteoporosis, prior seizure disorder or clear trauma, the authors diagnosed seizure-induced lumbar compression fractures, with features of a possible AO Spine A3 burst fracture at L4, and noted that the diagnosis was delayed because lumbar imaging was not done at the first encounter.

After neurosurgery consultation, balloon kyphoplasty with cement augmentation was performed at L1, L4 and L5 for persistent severe pain and imaging evidence of instability without neurologic compromise or canal stenosis. Postoperative radiographs showed cement within the treated vertebral bodies, restored height and no extravasation, retropulsion or canal compromise. Pain improved to near resolution with no new reported seizures, and the two-week outpatient examination showed intact cranial nerves, full (5/5) lower-extremity strength, symmetric 2+ reflexes, steady gait and no focal neurologic deficits.
